A gaffe is an embarrassing mistake you make in a social situation — usually by saying or doing something inappropriate, offensive, or clumsy, without meaning to.

The "without meaning to" part is crucial. A gaffe is always an accident. The person who makes it typically wishes they could take it back the moment it happens.

For something to be a gaffe, it usually has three ingredients:

1. It's a social error, not just any mistake.
If you miscalculate a math problem, that's a mistake — but not a gaffe. A gaffe happens in the presence of other people, in a conversation, a public setting, or a social situation. It's the kind of error that makes people around you go quiet or cringe.

2. It's unintentional.
The person didn't mean to cause offense or embarrassment. They may have spoken without thinking, misjudged the situation, or simply said the wrong thing at the wrong moment.

3. It causes embarrassment or awkwardness — usually for the person who made it.
Sometimes a gaffe offends the people around them too. But the defining mark of a gaffe is that socially, something has gone wrong.

Here are situations where the word "gaffe" fits perfectly:

  • You meet your friend's new partner for the first time. Trying to be friendly, you say, "Oh, you're so much better-looking than his ex!" — You meant it as a compliment, but it was a gaffe. It was awkward, unnecessary, and made everyone uncomfortable.
  • At a dinner party, you ask a woman, "When are you due?" — assuming she's pregnant. She's not. That's a painful gaffe.
  • You forget someone's name at an important meeting and loudly call them by the wrong name in front of a crowd. Gaffe.
  • You text your boss complaining about your boss — and realize, too late, that you sent it to your boss. That's a classic gaffe.

The word "gaffe" is extremely common in politics, journalism, and public life, because public figures are watched closely and every misstep gets attention.

  • A politician accidentally insults a group of voters while trying to flatter them.
  • A company's spokesperson makes an offensive joke during a live press conference.
  • A celebrity forgets the name of the film they starred in during an interview.

In fact, there's a famous (and somewhat humorous) observation that a political gaffe is when a politician accidentally says what they actually think — something they weren't supposed to admit in public.
How Is a Gaffe Different from Similar Words?

Since you want to fully understand this word, it helps to see how it compares to words that feel similar:

Mistake — A general word for any error. You can make a mistake in cooking, in driving, in math. A gaffe is a specific kind of mistake: a social one.

Blunder — A bigger, clumsier mistake. A blunder can be social or professional, and often implies something more serious. Every gaffe can be called a blunder, but not every blunder is a gaffe.

Faux pas — This is the closest word to gaffe. A faux pas is also an unintentional social mistake that violates the rules of polite behavior. In everyday use, the two words are nearly interchangeable. If there's a fine difference, it's this: a faux pas tends to be about breaking the rules of etiquette (e.g., using the wrong fork at a formal dinner, or not RSVPing to a wedding), while a gaffe often involves saying the wrong thing. But this line is blurry, and most native speakers use them interchangeably.

Slip — A small, often verbal, accidental error (a "slip of the tongue"). A slip is usually minor and forgivable. A gaffe carries more social weight and embarrassment.

Here are natural ways you'll see and hear "gaffe" used:

  • "He made a terrible gaffe at the dinner party."
  • "Her gaffe was caught on camera and went viral."
  • "The senator's gaffe cost him support among younger voters."
  • "It was an embarrassing gaffe that he'll never live down."
  • "Despite a few gaffes early in his career, he became a respected speaker."

You "make" a gaffe or "commit" a gaffe. You don't "do" a gaffe or "have" a gaffe.

A gaffe is an unintentional social blunder — usually something said (or sometimes done) that turns out to be embarrassing, offensive, or awkward. It's not about being stupid or bad; even intelligent, careful people make gaffes. What makes it a gaffe is that it happened in a social setting, it wasn't meant to cause harm, and it left people cringing. The bigger the audience, the more memorable the gaffe.
